opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more underrated levers we have. Right now most model safeguards operate as if every request arrives in a vacuum: the model sees a single prompt, maybe a bit of conversation context, and has to decide whether to help. That's a hard problem, because so much of what's genuinely dangerous looks almost identical to what's legitimate. A question about pathogen enhancement techniques could come from a vaccine researcher or from someone with bad intentions, and the text alone often doesn't distinguish them.

Account history changes the problem. If you know a user has been on the platform for two years, works in an institutional setting, has a pattern of asking coherent research-adjacent questions, and maybe has gone through some kind of verification, that's real evidence. It lets you shift the threshold. You can be more generous with that person and more cautious with a brand-new anonymous account that suddenly jumps straight to the most sensitive material.

It also helps on the other side. Many attacks we see aren't a single malicious prompt; they're decomposition attacks, where someone breaks a harmful task into innocuous-looking pieces spread across many queries or even many accounts. You can only catch that if you're looking at patterns over time rather than individual requests.

That said, there are real tradeoffs. Privacy is the obvious one: you're building a profile of users, and that data has to be handled carefully. There's also a fairness concern, since reputation systems tend to favor people who are already well-resourced or institutionally affiliated, and you don't want to lock out independent researchers or people in less-represented countries. And sophisticated adversaries will try to game it by aging accounts, building fake reputations, or buying compromised ones. So I don't see it as a silver bullet, but as one layer in a defense-in-depth approach. It's often much more informative than anything you can extract from the prompt alone.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more underrated levers we have, and it's worth stepping back to see why. Right now, when a model gets a borderline request, something like "how does this piece of malware work" or "what dose of this drug is dangerous," it's basically making a decision in a vacuum. It sees one message, maybe a short conversation, and it has to guess at intent with almost no information. And the consequence is that it's either going to be too permissive for the small fraction of actually malicious users, or too restrictive for the overwhelming majority of people with totally legitimate reasons: security researchers, clinicians, students, journalists. You can't really resolve that tradeoff at the level of a single prompt, because the prompt just doesn't contain enough signal.

Account history changes that picture. If someone has been using a system for a year to do penetration testing work, has a verified affiliation with a security firm, and has never tripped any wires, then a question about exploit development looks very different than the same question from an account created twenty minutes ago that's already probed a bunch of different harmful topics. That's how we handle this in basically every other high-stakes domain. A pharmacist treats a regular customer with a documented prescription differently from a stranger paying cash for the same thing. It's not perfect, but it's a lot more information than nothing.

I'd put the benefits into a few buckets. One is just better calibration, the model's uncertainty about intent goes down, so you get fewer false refusals and fewer false permits at the same time. Two is that it raises the cost of misuse. If a bad actor needs to build up months of benign history before they can get access to more sensitive capabilities, that's real friction, and it makes the whole "spin up a thousand throwaway accounts" strategy much less attractive. Three, and I think this is important, it lets you shift some of the burden off the model. A lot of the current approach puts enormous weight on the model's in-context judgment, which is fragile and easy to jailbreak. Reputation lets you make the hard decisions at the system level, where you can have audits and human review and rate limits and so on.

That said, I want to be honest about the failure modes, because there are several and they're not trivial. The obvious one is that reputation systems can be gamed. People will build up history specifically to launder later requests, or buy aged accounts, the same way they do on every other platform. So you can't treat long history as a free pass, it's a prior, not a verdict. The second is a sort of equity problem. Who gets a good reputation? People who already have institutional affiliations, who've been on the platform longer, who happen to be in jurisdictions with good identity infrastructure. A grad student in a country with weaker verification might get locked out of legitimate research that someone at a wealthy Western university accesses freely. That's a real cost and I don't think we should wave it away.

And then there's the privacy and concentration piece. A system that makes judgments based on your entire interaction history is also a system that's keeping your entire interaction history, and that's being run by a handful of companies. I'd want to see that done with a lot of care: clear limits on what's retained, what it's used for, meaningful ways to contest a bad judgment, ideally some externalization so it's not just one lab deciding who's trustworthy.

So my overall view is that it's clearly directionally right. The current model of adjudicating every borderline request as if it's from an anonymous stranger is leaving a lot of value on the table and it's also not that safe. But I'd want to see it implemented as one layer among several, with reputation shifting the threshold rather than replacing the judgment, and with real attention paid to who ends up on the wrong side of the line. The thing I'd caution against is treating this as the thing that solves dual-use. It's a helpful piece of a layered defense, and when people start saying "we can just rely on verified users," that's usually a sign they haven't thought hard enough about how the adversary adapts.

astra-6.text:
I think the key idea is that you shouldn’t have to judge every request in isolation. The same question could be coming from a security researcher trying to fix a vulnerability or from someone trying to exploit it. If you only see the question, there may simply not be enough information to distinguish those cases.

Account history could give you useful context. Has this person been working on a coherent defensive project? Have previous interactions given you reason to trust them, or have they repeatedly tried to get around safeguards? That could help systems make more calibrated decisions, rather than either refusing everything potentially risky or answering everything.

But reputation is evidence, not a guarantee. Accounts can be compromised, and someone can build up a benign history before making a harmful request. You also don’t want a system where new users can’t get useful help because they haven’t established a reputation yet. So I’d see it as one input into the judgment, alongside the actual request and the consequences of providing assistance, rather than a blanket exemption for trusted users.

sol-6.1.text:
I think account history can give you useful context that’s missing when you look at a request in isolation. The same technical question might be part of a legitimate research project or one step in doing something harmful. If you have a history of someone working on a coherent project, that can help you interpret what they’re asking for.

But I’d be cautious about treating reputation as a blanket exemption. Accounts can be compromised, and someone could build up a benign history before making a harmful request. Conversely, a new user shouldn’t automatically be treated as malicious. So I’d see it as one signal among several, alongside the content of the request and what capabilities the answer would actually provide.

The interesting possibility is that this lets us make more nuanced decisions: ask a clarifying question, provide a safer version of the assistance, or allow more detail when there’s good reason to believe it’s appropriate. The challenge is getting that benefit without creating a system where established users get unlimited trust and everyone else is locked out.
